title: Dana White Slams Oscar De La Hoya, Blames Vince McMahon for “Set‑Up” in Garcia‑Benn Fight Scandal
body:
The UFC’s top executive, Dana White, has publicly dismissed former boxing champion Oscar De La Hoya’s allegation that the promoter deliberately “set up” the fighter‑pay dispute surrounding the cancelled bout between Gervonta Garcia and Ryan Benn. In a candid interview, White not only refuted the claim but also recounted a personal anecdote about being the victim of a similar backstage maneuver by WWE mogul Vince McMahon, underscoring the long‑standing tension between the two combat‑sport icons.

White’s rebuttal came after De La Hoya, who has been vocal about his frustrations with the UFC’s handling of the Garcia‑Benn fight, suggested that the organization engineered the cancellation to protect its own interests. “I would never disrespect Oscar at a fight I’m promoting,” White said, emphasizing that the UFC had no intention of sabotaging the matchup. He noted that the cancellation stemmed from legitimate contractual and medical concerns, not a covert plot. According to White, the fighters’ camps were unable to agree on a unified purse structure, and a late‑stage injury to Benn forced the promotion’s hand. “We tried to make it work,” White added, “but the reality is that sometimes the stars don’t align, and you have to make a tough call.”

The dispute reignited a feud that stretches back years. De La Hoya, who transitioned from a decorated boxing career to promoting his own “Fight Club” events, has repeatedly criticized the UFC for what he perceives as monopolistic practices. The tension escalated last month when De La Hoya’s promotion announced a tentative deal with Garcia, only for the UFC to step in and claim exclusive rights to the fighter’s next bout. While De La Hoya framed the situation as a “set‑up,” White argued that the UFC’s contractual clauses simply preempted any cross‑promotion, a standard practice in the industry.

In an unexpected twist, White drew a parallel to a personal experience with Vince McMahon, the late wrestling titan who once attempted to poach a UFC talent for a cross‑promotional event. White recounted how McMahon, impressed by the UFC’s rising profile, invited a top‑ranked fighter to appear on a WWE pay‑per‑view. The UFC, fearing a loss of control over its athletes, renegotiated the agreement at the last minute, leaving the wrestler’s team feeling “set up.” “It was a lesson in how power dynamics work in combat sports,” White said, implying that the Garcia‑Benn saga was no different in principle—just a matter of who holds the leverage at a given moment.

Analysts see White’s anecdote as a strategic move to shift the narrative from a personal grievance to a broader commentary on the business realities of mixed martial arts and boxing. The UFC’s exclusive contracts have long been a point of contention for rival promoters, who argue that they stifle competition and limit fighters’ earning potential. Conversely, UFC officials maintain that such agreements protect the brand’s integrity and ensure consistent event quality. The Garcia‑Benn cancellation, therefore, may become a case study in how contractual rigidity can clash with the fluid nature of fight negotiations.

Looking ahead, both organizations appear poised to recalibrate their approaches. De La Hoya’s promotion has hinted at exploring alternative venues and partners to circumvent UFC exclusivity, while the UFC is reportedly reviewing its talent‑sharing policies after a wave of criticism from fighters and fans alike. The episode underscores a shifting landscape where traditional boxing promoters and the rapidly expanding MMA industry must navigate a delicate balance between collaboration and competition. Whether the two sides will find common ground or continue their rivalry remains to be seen, but the fallout from the Garcia‑Benn debacle is likely to influence future cross‑sport negotiations for months to come.
